title: 34-year-old with sudden right arm tremor and posturing after a minor wrist injury, worse in the evenings

provenance.citation: Synthetic case drafted 2026-10-17 for Rare Disease Detective; not derived from any individual patient.

chief_complaint: "My right hand started shaking and clenching after I sprained my wrist, and it's worse by the evening."
history_of_present_illness: Eight months ago she sprained her right wrist in a fall. Within a week, abrupt onset of right-hand tremor that reached its maximum severity within days. Over the following months, intermittent clenched-fist posturing of the right hand developed. Symptoms vary considerably day to day, with some completely symptom-free hours, and are worse by evening and when tired; better on holiday. She has read about dopa-responsive dystonia online and asks whether she should be tested. Comorbid migraine and a past episode of depression, currently well. High work stress after a recent promotion.

symptom_timeline.event: Abrupt-onset right-hand tremor, maximal within days
Two weeks of complete remission during holiday, then recurrence

movement_findings.observation: Right-hand tremor 5–7 Hz with marked variability in frequency and axis across examination.
Entrainment: when tapping a 3 Hz rhythm with the left hand, right tremor shifts to 3 Hz; when asked to stop tapping, tremor resumes at original frequency.
Distractibility: tremor stops during serial-7 subtraction and fine left-hand tasks.
Clenched-fist posture of the right hand, which can be passively opened with resistance that varies, and resolves fully when she is distracted.
Co-activation sign present at the wrist at tremor onset.

neurological_exam.power: Collapsing 'give-way' weakness of right grip; Hoover-type sign not applicable (upper limb)
neurological_exam.bradykinesia_screen: Slow right finger tapping without decrement, improves with encouragement

family_history: Cousin with 'dystonia' (type unknown, cervical, onset in 50s). Otherwise negative.
prior_workup_and_opinions: GP: 'possible early Parkinson's or dystonia, refer.'
